The Set Product at a Glance

Learn these identifiers cold — examiners reward precise reference to this edition.

The Big Issue, No. 1227 — Special 25th Anniversary Edition, 17–23 Oct 2016
Founders
John Bird & Gordon Roddick (1991)
Publisher
The Big Issue Company Ltd, in partnership with Dennis Publishing
Genre
Current affairs & entertainment (genre hybrid)
Type
Non-mainstream / alternative · social enterprise, not-for-profit

£2.50 (vendor buys at £1.25, keeps £1.25)

Why it exists — the ideology The Big Issue is a business solution to a social problem: it offers homeless and vulnerably-housed people a legitimate income ("a hand up, not a handout"). Its whole media language, industry model and representations flow from this ethos — vendors are shown as workers, not beggars.

M Media Language

How the codes and conventions of a magazine construct meaning — masthead, strapline, cover lines, image, mode of address, colour and layout.

Conventions of a magazine cover — and how this one plays them

Rule of thirds & the Z-line Convention: masthead (top third), key image (middle third), main cover line/banners (bottom third); the eye travels in a "Z" across the masthead, down and across the base. Mainstream titles conform closely; alternative titles are more likely to subvert these codes.
  • Masthead — the iconic red-and-black "THE BIG ISSUE" logo, top-centre, gives instant brand identity at the newsstand/street.
  • Strapline — "A hand up not a handout" sits directly under the masthead, unusually foregrounding the magazine's social mission rather than a cover story.
  • No conventional cover lines — the anniversary special drops them, signalling this issue is different / important and letting the celebratory image dominate.
  • Central image — a Las-Vegas-style illuminated "25 years" marquee; warm orange/gold light-bulbs against a dark sky connote a party, celebration and spectacle ("a publishing revolution").
  • Colour palette — warm, bright, high-contrast to catch the eye "at a distance" on the street (Art Director Ross Lesley-Bayne's own point).
  • Banners — celebrity list (Andy Murray, Theresa May, the Dalai Lama…) plus "THOUSANDS & THOUSANDS of vendors" balances mainstream pull with the magazine's community.
Anchorage (Barthes) Every image is fixed in meaning by text. On the contents page the speech bubble "Hello, my name is Donato" anchors the smiling vendor as an individual with a story — turning a statistic into a person.

Binary oppositions on the cover & manifesto (Lévi-Strauss)

The slogan sets up a structuring set of oppositions that carry the magazine's whole ethos:

hand up
vs
handout
working
vs
begging
independence
vs
dependency
social enterprise
vs
charity
Evaluation move Push beyond spotting oppositions: ask whether a purely binaristic reading is too simplistic. Where do binaries break down? (e.g. Grayson Perry destabilises the masculine/feminine binary.)

The Set Extracts — analysed

These are the pages you must be able to reference precisely. Tap any page to read the detail.

Contents page (p.3) — "Hello, my name is Donato"

  • Layout: contents list on the left lets the reader choose; but the large image of Donato is the first thing the eye meets.
  • Mode of address: the speech-bubble "Hello, my name is Donato" is direct and informal — personal, warm.
  • Mise-en-scène: the distinctive red bib and lanyard signify a legitimate vendor — readers know only these sellers are official.
  • The Manifesto ("WE BELIEVE…"): unconventional for a contents page — it's social, not consumer-driven, telling readers exactly where their money goes.
  • Values: emotive personal narrative ("I now have a roof over my head") makes poverty relatable and dignified.

Editor's Letter (p.6) — "This is a milestone. Where will it take us?"

  • Font/design: dense, small, black serif copy reads as serious, formal, "quality" journalism.
  • Mode of address: shifts from indirect (facts — "In 1991, Bob Dylan didn't have a Nobel Prize… Amazon was simply a river") to direct ("we must also seek to speak for those still ignored").
  • Rhetorical device: the archive headline "but why don't the homeless just go home?" — a rhetorical question that framed the very first edition.
  • Image: black-and-white reproduction of the first cover signals heritage and the 25-year journey.
  • Narrative: then → now → future ("we will fight for those without access to books"), giving context and forward mission.

Feature: 'Letter to My Younger Self — Grayson Perry' (p.14–15)

  • Images: a colourful mid/establishing shot; bold primary colours make it playful and inviting; the second page shows Perry full-length in an artwork dress.
  • Pull quote: "The Daily Mail would be happy to know they facilitated my sexual fetish" — humorous, provocative, anchors image and text.
  • Mode of address: conversational, direct, as if speaking to us; the ironic "textbook dad" tag (he is anything but typical).
  • Representation / values: a positive, empowering portrait; a voice for the LGBTQ+ community; challenges toxic / narrow masculinity — the moral is to be who you are.

Feature: 'Vendor Success Stories — Moving On' (p.32–33, 35)

  • Headline & standfirst: "Moving On" (top-left) with a standfirst anchoring the theme — vendors who used the magazine as a stepping stone.
  • Layout: columns anchor each portrait to its story, making success feel personal and real.
  • Images: a range of ethnicities and backgrounds in mid- and wide-shots, in the settings where they now work.
  • Values: aspirational, hopeful — reinforces "a hand up, not a handout"; challenges the misrepresentation of homeless people as helpless.

Feature: 'Rise of the Homeless Bakers — No Soggy Bottoms Here!' (p.41)

  • Genre hybridity in action: uses the mainstream appeal of The Great British Bake Off (celebrity/entertainment) as a vehicle for social commentary — a social enterprise, Rise Bakery, tackling the root causes of homelessness.
  • Mode of address: witty, punning headline; warm, human-interest tone.
  • Values: shows entertainment content being reconciled with the magazine's social purpose.
Genre debateCritics argue celebrity content detracts from the message of inequality; the publishers argue it broadens the audience and raises more revenue for vendors. This article is the model answer to that tension.

Feature: 'My Pitch' (p.58) — Donato Barbieri, 70

  • Headline: "The Big Issue gave an old man like me a sense of purpose again" — emotive, first-person, dignifying.
  • Structure: a "Facts about me" sidebar humanises the vendor; direct address throughout.
  • Representation: gives the homeless a voice — the same Donato who fronts the contents page, bookending the issue with the vendor community at its heart.

Adverts (at least 3 key adverts)

Advertising must be read for audience (VALs), how they target through techniques, and representation. Note the high proportion of charity / public-information ads — they reinforce the magazine's ethos.

  • Chain of Hope (children's cardiac charity): targets ethically-aware reformers; emotive image of carer & child — links to maternal / nurturing female representation (staged photo).
  • redmolotov.com ("Coexist", "Rebel not Slave"): ethical, politically-engaged clothing — appeals to the socially-conscious ABC1 reader; reinforces the counter-cultural brand identity.
  • Southdown Duvets / D-Mannose / Adoption: a mix of ethical consumer goods, health and public-information ads — matching an older, caring, ABC1 audience rather than luxury/aspirational brands (contrast with Vogue).
Symbiotic relationshipAdvertising is ~one third of magazine revenue, so ads must "deliver" the same audience to advertisers. The kind of ads a magazine carries is itself evidence of who its readers are.

I Industry

Ownership & control, economic factors, and regulation of the magazine industry.

Mainstream vs Alternative media

Mainstream

Large-scale, aimed at big homogenous audiences · commercial / state organisations · vertically-structured, staffed by professionals · carriers of dominant discourses. (e.g. Vogue)

Alternative

Small-scale, aimed at specific / disadvantaged communities · independent of state & market · horizontally-structured (audience access & participation) · carriers of non-dominant / counter-hegemonic discourses. (e.g. The Big Issue)

Nuance for top marksThese are historically relative concepts — what's alternative in one era can become mainstream in another. The Big Issue is alternative in ethos but uses mainstream celebrity content — a hybrid.

Ownership & the social-enterprise model

  • Published in partnership with Dennis Publishing, an independent media company that provides subbing, production, design and generates advertising revenue.
  • Dennis was later sold to private-equity firm Exponent for £150m (proceeds to the Heart of England Forest charity) — useful evidence when evaluating ownership.
  • The Big Issue Group has three arms: the magazine, Big Issue Invest (social investment) and The Big Issue Foundation (charitable arm), plus an online shop.
  • How the money works: vendors buy each copy for £1.25 and sell for £2.50 — earning £1.25 per copy — a business model, not a handout.

Economic factors & distribution

  • Revenue = sales (print + digital) + advertising (~one third of industry revenue).
  • Not widely sold in mainstream retail — sold on the street by vendors, so a striking cover must "draw people in at a distance."
  • Digital distribution via Zinio (6,000+ titles, ~10m readers, any device) reaches audiences the street model can't — and digital revenue funds further vendor support.
  • Wider industry context: falling print circulation, rising digital, closures (Nuts, Loaded), and a shift to niche titles with a unique selling point and loyal audience.

Regulation

  • The UK press is self-regulated (largely by IPSO). Print is easier to regulate than online.
  • The internet is hard to regulate: it's global (national action is easily circumvented), no single body controls it, and content can't truly be erased. Globalisation — Big Issue downloads worldwide via Zinio — complicates jurisdiction.

A Audience

How the magazine categorises, targets, reaches, addresses and constructs its audience — and how audiences use and interpret it.

Gender split
~50/50 male & female
Average age
46
Social grade
72% ABC1 · 43% AB
Values
Socially, ethically & environmentally aware — "reformers"

Mass and specialised

Though non-mainstream, the Big Issue targets both: its ethics and social purpose appeal to reformers (VALs), while celebrity, entertainment and popular culture pull in a more mainstream audience. Social media alerts readers to new issues, drives traffic to the website and uses hashtags to encourage participation — and to reach a younger, digital-only demographic who see vendors on the street but might not buy print.

Uses & Gratifications (Blumler & Katz)

Information / Surveillance

Current affairs, social issues, long-form journalism and reportage not found on the website.

Personal Identity

Readers align with the magazine's ethical, socially-conscious values.

Entertainment / Diversion

Celebrity interviews (Grayson Perry), culture, the "lean-back" pleasure of relaxing with the mag.

Social Interaction + "Halo effect"

Andy Cowles' point: the good feeling of supporting a vendor spills over into the pleasure of reading (the "halo effect").

Constructing the audience — Gerbner (Cultivation) Repeated exposure to the magazine's patterns of representation can cultivate readers' view of the world — here, shaping attitudes to homelessness and social inequality and challenging dominant discourses.
Interpreting it — Stuart Hall (Reception) Readers decode the same text differently: a preferred reading (homelessness deserves compassion & a hand up), a negotiated one, or an oppositional one (celebrity content undermines the message). Interpretation reflects age, gender, class and cultural capital.

R Representation

How and why particular social groups and issues are represented — homelessness, gender, and race/ethnicity.

Homelessness & poverty (the central issue)

  • Directly counters the under-representation and misrepresentation of homeless people in mainstream media.
  • Vendors are represented as dignified workers with names, faces and stories (Donato, the Moving On success stories) — not passive victims.
  • The magazine invokes discourses of self-help, opportunity and social justice, positioning readers to view homelessness with compassion and as a solvable social problem.

Gender

  • Grayson Perry — diverse, fluid masculinity; supports Gauntlett's claim that we no longer get single, straightforward messages about male/female identity.
  • Moving On / Soggy Bottom bakers — men who "should" be providers but have fallen on hard times, now active and rebuilding; still, more male stories than female.
  • Chain of Hope advert — a singular, maternal, caring female constructed through a staged photo — a more conventional gender representation.
  • Van Zoonen / bell hooks: women in the selected pages tend to be more posed/passive (e.g. Marvina — bright colours, decorative) than the active men on motorbikes.

Race & ethnicity

  • The magazine industry under-represents BAME groups, often blamed on the lack of ethnic diversity among those who work in it.
  • In the selected pages, 17% of people are from a BAME background vs 13% of the population (2011 census) — arguably more representative than the norm.
  • Stuart Hall's "burden of representation": under-represented groups carry extra cultural weight, standing in for a whole group — raising the risk of stereotyping. Hall calls for positive images to substitute for negative ones.

C Contexts

Social, cultural, historical, economic & political circumstances that shaped the product.

Social & Cultural

Homelessness, poverty and austerity in the UK; rising rough sleeping. The magazine exists to give a voice to a marginalised group.

Historical

Founded 1991 (inspired by New York's Street News); this issue marks 25 years — "a publishing revolution." The editor situates 1991 (Bob Dylan, Gorbachev, "Amazon was simply a river").

Political

2016 Britain — post-EU-referendum, Theresa May as PM (she features in the birthday messages). Campaigning content, e.g. Stop the FOBTs (Owen Baily). A counter-hegemonic, socially-committed stance.

Economic

Print circulation falling / digital rising; the social-enterprise model turns commercial pressure into vendor income.

Theories — mapped to The Big Issue

The named theorists you can apply. Use them to evaluate, not just label.

Media Language
Barthes — Semiotics

Denotation/connotation & anchorage. "Hello, my name is Donato" anchors the vendor image.

Media Language / Rep
Lévi-Strauss — Structuralism

Binary oppositions: hand up/handout, working/begging, independence/dependency.

Industry
Curran & Seaton

Power is concentrated in a few profit-driven firms. Evaluate: Big Issue is a not-for-profit social enterprise — an exception that challenges the theory.

Industry
Hesmondhalgh — Cultural Industries

Companies minimise risk & maximise audiences. Big Issue instead prioritises social value.

Audience
Blumler & Katz — Uses & Gratifications

Information, identity, entertainment, social interaction (the "halo effect").

Audience
Gerbner — Cultivation

Repeated exposure shapes attitudes to homelessness & inequality.

Audience
Stuart Hall — Reception

Preferred / negotiated / oppositional readings.

Representation
David Gauntlett — Identity

"No longer singular, straightforward messages" about gender — Grayson Perry supports this.

Representation
Liesbet van Zoonen — Feminism

Gender is constructed; women often positioned as passive/decorative (e.g. Moving On, adverts).

Representation
bell hooks — Feminism

Beauty ideals; women "socialised to believe sexist thinking" too; calls for healthy alternatives.

Representation
Stuart Hall — Representation

The "burden of representation" & substituting positive images.

Representation
Alvarado, Gutch & Wollen

Racial stereotypes: the exotic, dangerous, humorous, pitied.

Exam essentials Component 2, Section B is worth 30 marks. Expect either a two-part question or one extended-response essay across both set products (Big Issue + Vogue). Practice questions from your lessons:
  • "Explore how the set edition of The Big Issue conveys viewpoints and ideologies. [15]"
  • "To what extent does the set edition of The Big Issue target a particular audience? [15]"
  • Gauntlett — evaluate "we no longer get singular, straightforward messages about ideal types of male and female identities" re The Big Issue. [15]
  • Curran & Seaton — evaluate this theory of power & media industries, referring to Vogue and The Big Issue. [15]
Top-band answers evaluate the validity of a theory with a sustained, substantiated line of reasoning — not just describe.

Key Terms

Social enterprise

A business that trades to achieve a social mission and reinvests profits into that cause — the Big Issue's core model.

Counter-hegemonic

Challenging the dominant ideology. The Big Issue counters mainstream discourses about homelessness.

Anchorage

(Barthes) The way text fixes the meaning of an image, reducing its possible interpretations.

Mode of address

How a text "speaks" to its audience — direct/indirect, formal/informal. The Big Issue often uses direct, informal address.

Genre hybridity

Combining conventions of more than one genre — here, current affairs and entertainment.

Binary opposition

(Lévi-Strauss) Meaning built from opposing pairs, e.g. "a hand up / a handout."

Burden of representation

(Hall) When few members of a group appear in the media, each carries the weight of representing the whole group.

Halo effect

The good feeling of a socially-positive purchase (supporting a vendor) enhancing the pleasure of the product.

ABC1

The upper social grades (professional/managerial to junior white-collar). 72% of Big Issue readers are ABC1.

VALs — Reformers

A values-based audience segment: idealistic, socially-conscious, questioning — the Big Issue's core readership.
